opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because when you look at the outputs today, it's easy to think the problem is solved. The images are photorealistic, the textures are beautiful, the lighting looks right. But once you start probing these models more carefully, a lot of gaps show up.

The first one I'd point to is compositionality and faithfulness to the prompt. If you ask for "a red cube on top of a blue sphere, to the left of a green cylinder," the models often mix up the attributes, swap the colors, or ignore the spatial relationships altogether. Counting is similar: ask for seven apples and you might get five or nine. The model understands the concepts individually, but binding attributes to the right objects and respecting relations between them is still quite fragile. A lot of that comes from how the text encoder and the cross-attention mechanism interact. Information from different tokens leaks into the wrong regions of the image.

The second area is controllability. Artists and designers don't just want a nice image. They want this particular layout, this pose, this identity preserved across multiple shots, this style kept consistent. We've made progress with conditioning on edges, depth, segmentation maps and so on, but fine-grained, intuitive editing is still clumsy. It's hard to say "move this object a little to the right and keep everything else the same" and actually have everything else stay the same.

Third, consistency, both across images and in 3D. If you generate a character and want them in ten different scenes, keeping identity, clothing and details stable is hard. And the images aren't really grounded in a coherent 3D world. You see it in shadows that don't match light sources, reflections that are slightly off, hands and geometric structures that break down. Physics and geometry are things the model approximates statistically rather than really understands.

Then there's efficiency. Diffusion models traditionally need many denoising steps, and these networks are huge. For on-device deployment, on a phone for example, you need to cut both the number of steps and the model size dramatically without losing quality. Distillation, few-step or one-step samplers, quantization, and smarter architectures are all active areas, and there's still a lot of room there.

Evaluation is another underappreciated problem. Metrics like FID or CLIP score don't really capture whether the image matches what the user asked for, or whether it's aesthetically good. We still rely heavily on human judgment, which is expensive and hard to scale. Better automatic evaluation, especially for compositional correctness, would accelerate the whole field.

And finally, the responsible side: bias in what the models generate, copyright and data provenance, preventing harmful content, watermarking and detection. These aren't just policy questions. They're real technical research problems.

So realism, in a sense, was the easier part. The harder part now is making these models precise, controllable, consistent, efficient, and trustworthy.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, Sam, it's great to be here. You're right that if you look at the samples coming out of the latest diffusion and autoregressive models, the photorealism question is largely solved in the sense that a casual viewer often can't tell. But I'd argue that realism was never really the hard part. It was the part that scales nicely with data and compute. The remaining challenges are mostly about everything around the pixels.

The first one is controllability and compositional understanding. If I ask for "a red cube on top of a blue sphere, to the left of a green cone," models still get the counting, the spatial relations, and the attribute binding wrong surprisingly often. They've learned the statistics of what images look like, but they don't have a strong, explicit notion of scene structure. Closing that gap probably requires better alignment between the language side and the visual side, maybe intermediate representations like layouts or 3D scene graphs, rather than just a bigger text encoder.

The second is consistency. Generating one beautiful image is easy; generating the same character, the same object, the same lighting across a sequence of images, or across edits, is hard. That's really the bridge from single images to video, to 3D, and to real production workflows, where an artist wants to iterate on one asset, not regenerate the whole scene every time.

Third is efficiency. The sampling cost of these models is still high, and on the device side, which is where a lot of my own work sits, we care about running this on a phone at interactive rates with a tight memory and power budget. So distillation, few-step sampling, quantization, architectures that are hardware-aware — these are not glamorous, but they determine whether this technology reaches people or stays in the data center.

And then there's the trust layer: provenance, watermarking, evaluation. Our metrics are honestly quite weak. FID tells you about distribution similarity, CLIP score tells you about rough text relevance, but neither captures whether the model did what the user actually meant. Building evaluation that reflects human intent, and making generated content attributable, feels like unfinished research with real consequences.

So I'd summarize it this way: we've gotten very good at making images that look right. The next decade is about making images that are right — correct, consistent, controllable, cheap, and accountable.

astra-6.text:
Realism is only one part of the problem. An image can look very convincing and still fail to represent what you asked for. If you describe several objects and specify their attributes and spatial relationships, can the model get all of those details right? That compositional understanding remains a challenge.

Another issue is control. Suppose you like an image but want to change one small thing. Can you make that change while preserving everything else—the identity of the person, the lighting, the background? For many applications, that consistency is just as important as producing a beautiful image in the first place.

And then there is efficiency. We want these models to generate high-quality results with less computation and memory. So I think there is still a lot of research ahead: making generation more faithful to our intentions, more controllable, and more practical to use.

sol-6.1.text:
Realism is only one part of the problem. An image can look very convincing, but when you compare it with the prompt, you may find that it hasn’t actually captured what you asked for. If you specify several objects, their attributes, and their spatial relationships, can the model get all of those right? That compositional understanding is still a challenge.

Another important direction is controllability. You might generate an image you like and then want to change one thing—the position of an object, for example—while keeping everything else consistent. We need better ways to make those precise edits and give users more control over the generation process.

And there is a question of how we evaluate these systems. Visual quality alone doesn’t tell us whether the image follows the instructions or whether the model is reliable across different situations. So I think there is still a lot of research to do in moving from impressive image generation to tools that people can use predictably.
